tests.title: Unit 7: Analysis of Market Structure – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: In economics, a market refers to:
options: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers are in contact to exchange a good
questions.explanation: It need not be a fixed place.

questions.question_text: According to Cournot, a market is:
options: The entire region in which buyers and sellers are in such free intercourse that prices tend to equality
questions.explanation: The key idea is one price for the same good.

questions.question_text: Which is an essential of a market?
options: A commodity, buyers and sellers, and contact between them
questions.explanation: Also a price for the commodity.

questions.question_text: A market is always a physical place:
options: False; markets can be online or by telephone
questions.explanation: Contact between buyers and sellers is enough.

questions.question_text: Markets based on area are:
questions.explanation: Classification is by geographical extent.

questions.question_text: Marshall classified markets by time into:
options: Very short period, short period, long period and secular period
questions.explanation: Time determines how supply can adjust.

questions.question_text: On the basis of competition, markets are:
questions.explanation: Imperfect includes monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

questions.question_text: Wholesale markets differ from retail markets in that wholesale deals in:
options: Large quantities with traders; retail sells small quantities to consumers
questions.explanation: Retailers are the final link to consumers.

questions.question_text: Spot markets differ from future markets in that spot market transactions are:
options: Settled immediately; futures are for delivery at a later date
questions.explanation: Futures fix prices in advance.

questions.question_text: Which factor determines market structure?
options: Number of buyers and sellers, product type and entry barriers
questions.explanation: These define the degree of competition.

questions.question_text: Which market structure has a single seller?
questions.explanation: Others have many or few sellers.

questions.question_text: Perfect competition is a market with:
options: Many buyers and sellers selling a homogeneous product, with free entry and exit
questions.explanation: No individual can influence price.

questions.question_text: Which is a feature of perfect competition?
questions.explanation: Also many sellers and homogeneous products.

questions.question_text: Products must be homogeneous in perfect competition so that:
options: Buyers do not prefer one seller, giving a single price
questions.explanation: Identical products must sell at the same price.

questions.question_text: Free entry and exit is essential because:
options: It ensures only normal profit in the long run
questions.explanation: Supernormal profit attracts entrants.

questions.question_text: A firm is a price taker in perfect competition because:
options: Its output is a tiny share of the market
questions.explanation: It must accept the market price.

questions.question_text: The demand curve for a competitive firm is horizontal because:
options: It can sell any quantity at the market price
questions.explanation: It is perfectly elastic at that price.

questions.question_text: AR = MR = P under perfect competition because:
options: Price is constant for all units
questions.explanation: Each unit sells at the same price.

questions.question_text: Pure competition differs from perfect competition in that pure competition lacks:
questions.explanation: It is a narrower concept.

questions.question_text: Under perfect competition, price is determined by:
questions.explanation: The firm takes the price.

questions.question_text: Price is determined by the industry and not the firm because:
options: The firm's output is negligible relative to the market
questions.explanation: No single firm can change market supply.

questions.question_text: Short-run equilibrium of a competitive firm requires:
options: MR = MC and MC rising at that output
questions.explanation: Price = MC at equilibrium.

questions.question_text: Supernormal profit in the short run is when:
questions.explanation: AR is above AC.

questions.question_text: Normal profit in the short run is when:
questions.explanation: AR just covers AC.

questions.question_text: A loss-making firm continues producing in the short run if:
questions.explanation: It covers variable costs and part of fixed costs.

tests.title: Unit 7: Analysis of Market Structure – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: A competitive firm shuts down when:
questions.explanation: It cannot cover variable costs.

questions.question_text: The firm's supply curve in perfect competition is:
options: The part of the MC curve above minimum AVC
questions.explanation: The firm supplies where P = MC.

questions.question_text: Long-run equilibrium of a competitive firm requires:
questions.explanation: It earns only normal profit.

questions.question_text: Firms earn only normal profit in the long run because:
options: Entry and exit eliminate supernormal profit or loss
questions.explanation: Entry competes profit away.

questions.question_text: If there are supernormal profits in the industry:
options: New firms enter, increasing supply and reducing price
questions.explanation: Profit falls until normal.

questions.question_text: If firms are making losses in the industry:
options: Some firms exit, reducing supply and raising price
questions.explanation: Exit continues until losses disappear.

questions.question_text: Perfect competition is efficient because:
options: Price equals MC and output is at minimum AC
questions.explanation: Both allocative and productive efficiency are achieved.

questions.question_text: A merit of perfect competition is:
options: Optimum use of resources and low prices
questions.explanation: It benefits consumers.

questions.question_text: A demerit of perfect competition is:
options: No product variety and little incentive for innovation
questions.explanation: All products are identical.

questions.question_text: A constant-cost industry is one in which:
options: Long-run costs remain the same as the industry expands
questions.explanation: An increasing-cost industry has rising costs; a decreasing-cost industry has falling costs.

questions.question_text: Perfect competition is:
options: Rare in reality; agriculture and stock markets come close
questions.explanation: Most markets are imperfect.

questions.question_text: Imperfect competition arises because of:
options: Product differentiation, few sellers or barriers to entry
questions.explanation: These give firms market power.

questions.question_text: Monopoly is a market with:
options: A single seller of a product with no close substitutes
questions.explanation: The seller is the industry.

questions.question_text: Which is a feature of monopoly?
options: Single seller and barriers to entry
questions.explanation: The monopolist is a price maker.

questions.question_text: A source of monopoly power is:
questions.explanation: Others: control of raw materials, economies of scale.

questions.question_text: Patents and copyrights create monopoly by:
options: Giving exclusive rights to produce or sell an invention or work
questions.explanation: They bar others from using the invention.

questions.question_text: A natural monopoly arises when:
options: Economies of scale make a single firm the cheapest supplier, e.g., electricity distribution
questions.explanation: It is cheaper for one firm to serve the market.

questions.question_text: Under monopoly, the AR and MR curves are:
options: Downward sloping, with MR below AR
questions.explanation: MR lies below AR.

questions.question_text: The monopolist's equilibrium condition is:
options: MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below
questions.explanation: He charges the price on the demand curve at that output.

questions.question_text: A monopolist earns supernormal profit when:
questions.explanation: The profit area is the rectangle between AR and AC.

questions.question_text: A monopolist:
options: Can incur losses if AR < AC at every output
questions.explanation: Demand may be too weak to cover cost.

questions.question_text: A monopolist operates in the elastic portion of demand because:
options: MR is positive only where Ed > 1, which is needed for MR = MC
questions.explanation: MC is positive.

questions.question_text: A monopolist has no supply curve because:
options: Output and price are decided together from the demand curve
questions.explanation: There is no unique price–quantity relationship.

questions.question_text: Price discrimination is:
options: Charging different prices for the same product to different buyers
questions.explanation: The price differences are not based on cost.

questions.question_text: A condition for price discrimination is:
options: Markets can be separated and elasticities differ
questions.explanation: Resale must be prevented.

tests.title: Unit 7: Analysis of Market Structure – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Third-degree price discrimination means:
options: Different prices for different groups of buyers/markets
questions.explanation: First-degree is perfect discrimination; second-degree depends on quantity.

questions.question_text: An example of price discrimination in India is:
options: Different cinema ticket prices for different groups or times
questions.explanation: Railways and electricity tariffs also discriminate.

questions.question_text: A discriminating monopolist decides prices by equating:
options: MC with the MR in each market
questions.explanation: Total MR = MC, and each market's MR equals MC.

questions.question_text: A higher price is charged in the market with:
questions.explanation: Buyers there are less sensitive to price.

questions.question_text: A merit of monopoly is:
options: Economies of scale and resources for research
questions.explanation: Large size may lower costs.

questions.question_text: A demerit of monopoly is:
options: Higher price, lower output and exploitation of consumers
questions.explanation: Monopoly restricts output.

questions.question_text: Deadweight loss under monopoly is:
options: The welfare loss because output is below the competitive level
questions.explanation: Gains from trade are lost.

questions.question_text: The government can regulate monopoly through:
options: Price controls, antitrust laws and taxation
questions.explanation: It can also nationalise the monopoly.

questions.question_text: The Competition Commission of India:
options: Prevents anti-competitive practices and promotes competition
questions.explanation: It enforces the Competition Act, 2002.

questions.question_text: Compared with perfect competition, monopoly has:
options: A downward-sloping demand curve and price above MC
questions.explanation: Price-taker versus price-maker.

questions.question_text: Price is higher and output lower in monopoly because:
options: The monopolist restricts output to raise price where MR = MC
questions.explanation: MR is below price.

questions.question_text: Monopolistic competition is a market with:
questions.explanation: Firms have some control over price.

questions.question_text: The theory of monopolistic competition was developed by:
options: Edward Chamberlin (and Joan Robinson on imperfect competition)
questions.explanation: Both published in 1933.

questions.question_text: A feature of monopolistic competition is:
questions.explanation: Entry and exit are free.

questions.question_text: Product differentiation means:
options: Making similar products appear different through brand, quality or packaging
questions.explanation: E.g., toothpaste, soaps.

questions.question_text: Selling costs differ from production costs in that selling costs:
options: Create or increase demand (e.g., advertising), while production costs create utility
questions.explanation: They shift the demand curve.

questions.question_text: Demand under monopolistic competition is more elastic than under monopoly because:
questions.explanation: Buyers can switch brands.

questions.question_text: Non-price competition includes:
questions.explanation: Firms compete on features other than price.

questions.question_text: Short-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition is at:
options: MR = MC, with supernormal profit, normal profit or loss possible
questions.explanation: The firm acts like a monopolist in the short run.

questions.question_text: Long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition has:
options: P = AC (normal profit) with the demand curve tangent to the AC curve
questions.explanation: Entry removes supernormal profit.

questions.question_text: Excess capacity arises because the firm produces:
options: Less than the output at minimum AC (optimum scale)
questions.explanation: Tangency occurs on the falling part of AC.

questions.question_text: The tangency solution means that in the long run:
options: The demand curve is tangent to the AC curve
questions.explanation: Profit is normal.

questions.question_text: A "group" in monopolistic competition means:
options: A set of firms producing close substitutes
questions.explanation: Chamberlin used the group instead of the industry.

questions.question_text: Compared with perfect competition, monopolistic competition has:
questions.explanation: Price is higher and output is lower.

questions.question_text: Compared with monopoly, monopolistic competition has:
questions.explanation: Demand is more elastic.

tests.title: Unit 7: Analysis of Market Structure – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Oligopoly is a market with:
questions.explanation: Firms are interdependent.

questions.question_text: A feature of oligopoly is:
questions.explanation: Each firm considers rivals' reactions.

questions.question_text: Types of oligopoly include:
questions.explanation: Based on product type and cooperation.

questions.question_text: Interdependence in oligopoly means:
options: A firm's decisions depend on its rivals' reactions
questions.explanation: Each firm's output and price affect others.

questions.question_text: Demand is indeterminate under oligopoly because:
questions.explanation: The firm cannot predict its demand curve.

questions.question_text: Prices are rigid in oligopoly because:
options: Firms fear price wars and avoid changing prices
questions.explanation: Price changes may trigger retaliation.

questions.question_text: The kinked demand curve shows that rivals:
options: Match price cuts but not price rises
Match price rises but not cuts
questions.explanation: Demand is elastic above the kink and inelastic below it.

questions.question_text: The kinked demand curve model was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Sweezy (1939).

questions.question_text: There is a gap in the MR curve of the kinked model because:
options: The two segments of demand have different slopes at the kink
questions.explanation: MR is discontinuous at the kinked output.

questions.question_text: The kinked demand curve explains price rigidity because:
options: MC can change within the gap without changing price or output
questions.explanation: Equilibrium stays at the kink.

questions.question_text: A limitation of the kinked demand model is that it:
options: Does not explain how the original price is determined
questions.explanation: It only explains rigidity.

questions.question_text: A cartel is:
options: A formal agreement among firms to fix price/output, e.g., OPEC
questions.explanation: It acts like a monopoly.

questions.question_text: Cartels are unstable because:
options: Members have an incentive to cheat by producing more
questions.explanation: Cheating undermines agreed quotas.

questions.question_text: Price leadership is when:
options: One firm sets the price and others follow
questions.explanation: Types include dominant, barometric and low-cost leadership.

questions.question_text: Collusive oligopoly is where:
options: Firms cooperate to fix price or output
questions.explanation: It can be formal (cartel) or informal.

questions.question_text: Non-collusive oligopoly is where:
options: Firms act independently, considering rivals' reactions
questions.explanation: The kinked demand model is an example.

questions.question_text: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's dominant strategy leads to:
options: An outcome worse for both than cooperating
questions.explanation: Both confess even though both would be better off staying silent.

questions.question_text: A Nash equilibrium is:
options: A position where no player can gain by changing strategy alone
questions.explanation: Each strategy is the best response to the other's.

questions.question_text: In Cournot's duopoly model, each firm:
options: Assumes the rival's output remains constant
questions.explanation: Each chooses output given rival's output.

questions.question_text: A duopoly is a market with:
questions.explanation: It is a special case of oligopoly.

questions.question_text: Monopsony is a market with:
options: A single buyer, e.g., a sugar mill buying cane from farmers
questions.explanation: The buyer has power over the price paid.

questions.question_text: Bilateral monopoly is where:
options: A single seller faces a single buyer
questions.explanation: Price depends on bargaining power.

questions.question_text: Advertising is important in oligopoly because:
options: Firms use non-price competition to avoid price wars
questions.explanation: It builds brand loyalty.

questions.question_text: Oligopoly differs from monopolistic competition in that oligopoly has:
questions.explanation: Barriers to entry are usually higher.

questions.question_text: The market structure most commonly found in the real world is:
questions.explanation: Most real markets have differentiated products and some market power.
